title: Benchmarking Post-Quantum TLS: Performance, Security, and Deployment Trade-offs of Hybrid Key Exchange and Authentication
abstract: Post-quantum migration in TLS introduces two distinct engineering problems: replacing classical key exchange with a quantum-resistant or hybrid mechanism, and replacing classical certificate authentication with post-quantum signatures. This study benchmarks those dimensions separately and jointly using TLS 1.3 configurations based on X25519, X25519MLKEM768, ECDSA P-256, and ML-DSA-65. The benchmark reports N=300 fresh handshakes per configuration and provides aggregate median and mean latency, p95 and p99 latency, server CPU time per successful handshake, TLS-record bytes through Finished, ClientHello size, and certificate DER size. Median latency increased from 0.66595 ms for X25519/ECDSA to 0.87666 ms with hybrid X25519MLKEM768 key exchange (31.6%), 1.52414 ms with ML-DSA-65 authentication (128.9%), and 1.62282 ms when both mechanisms were combined (143.7%). The hybrid key exchange increased the ClientHello from 188 to 1,364 bytes (625.5%), while the measured ML-DSA-65 certificate was 5,521 bytes versus 396 bytes for ECDSA P-256 (1,294.2%). In this benchmark, ML-DSA authentication produced the larger latency and server-CPU effect, while hybrid key exchange produced the clearest first-flight size increase. The study is limited to the evaluated configurations and controlled environment and does not claim universal Internet or production performance.

title: Benchmarking NIST-Standardized Post-Quantum Digital Signatures (ML-DSA-44) for Secure IoT Authentication
abstract: As the Internet of Things (IoT) expands to encompass billions of devices in critical sectors like smart grids, healthcare, and industrial automation, ensuring the authenticity of data is paramount. Currently, digital signatures such as RSA and ECDSA (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm) are the bedrock of IoT authentication. However, the theoretical advent of fault-tolerant quantum computers threatens to break these schemes using Shor's Algorithm, which would allow attackers to forge identities and hijack devices. To preempt this crisis, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) has standardized ML-DSA (Dilithium) as the primary Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) digital signature. While robust, there are concerns regarding its performance overhead on resource-constrained IoT hardware. This paper presents a comprehensive feasibility study of ML-DSA-44 (Dilithium2), the lightweight variant of the standard. Utilizing a cross-compiled ARM64 emulation environment (QEMU) to replicate modern IoT gateway architecture, we benchmarked the critical operations of Key Generation, Signing, and Verification. Our empirical results reveal a verification latency of just 0.507 milliseconds and a signing latency of 1.869 milliseconds. These findings confirm that post-quantum authentication is computationally feasible for modern IoT devices, enabling a secure transition to the quantum era without necessitating expensive hardware upgrades.

title: Peer Review #1 of "A lightweight and secure online/offline cross-domain authentication scheme for VANET systems in Industrial IoT (v0.2)"
abstract: In heterogeneous wireless networks, the industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) is an essential contributor to increasing productivity and effectiveness. However, in various domains, such as industrial wireless scenarios, small cell domains, and vehicular ad hoc networks, an efficient and stable authentication algorithm is required (VANET). Specifically, IoT vehicles deal with vast amounts of data transmitted between VANET entities in different domains in such a large-scale environment. Also, crossing from one territory to another may have the connectivity services down for a while, leading to service interruption because it is pervasive in remote areas and places with multipath obstructions. Hence, it is vulnerable to specific attacks (e.g., replay attacks, modification attacks, man-in-the-middle attacks, and insider attacks), making the system inefficient. Also, high processing data increases the computation and communication cost, leading to an increased workload in the system. Thus, to solve the above issues, we propose an online/offline lightweight authentication scheme for the VANET cross-domain system in IIoT to improve the security and efficiency of the VANET. The proposed scheme utilizes an efficient AES-RSA algorithm to achieve integrity and confidentiality of the message. The offline joining is added to avoid remote network intrusions and the risk of network service interruptions. The proposed work includes two different significant goals to achieve first, then secure message on which the data is transmitted and efficiency in a cryptographic manner. The Burrows Abdi Needham (BAN logic) logic is used to prove that this scheme is mutually authenticated. The system's security has been tested using the well-known AVISPA tool to evaluate and verify its security formally. The results show that the proposed scheme outperforms the ID-CPPA, AAAS, and HCDA schemes by 53%, 55%, and 47% respectively in terms of computation cost, and 65%, 83%, and 40% respectively in terms of communication cost.

title: Hybrid Adaptive Post-Quantum Cryptographic Framework (HybridMedPQC) with Optimized SPHINCS+ for Long-Term Medical Image Security
venue: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology
abstract: : Quantum-capable adversaries threaten the long-term integrity of medical images exchanged through PACS/DICOM workflows, while post-quantum signatures introduce storage and latency trade-offs. This paper proposes HybridMedPQC, a tier-adaptive hybrid signing framework that combines CNN-and DICOM-assisted Image Sensitivity Classification with a policy-driven Adaptive Algorithm Selection Engine. For each image, Layered Signature Generation produces an inner archival anchor (SPHINCS+ or Dilithium/Falcon) and an outer transport signature (Dilithium or Falcon) bound with an RFC3161 timestamp to enable outer-first fast verification. A Long-Term Re-signing Protocol maintains archival validity by chaining refreshed signatures to prior records. Projected evaluation on 1024×1024 images shows up to 91.9% signature overhead reduction for the Standard tier and 81.2% for the Sensitive tier, versus standalone SPHINCS+, while preserving Falcon-level verification (~6–8 ms) and perfect image fidelity (SSIM=1.0, MSE=0, PSNR=∞). Critical-tier images retain NIST Level 5 defense-in-depth via SPHINCS+ plus Dilithium.

title: Quantum Shield: Design, Implementation, and Empirical Evaluation of a Hybrid Post-Quantum Secure Peer-to-Peer Communication System Using ML-KEM and ML-DSA
venue: Indian Journal of Computer Science and Technology
abstract: The emergence of fault-tolerant quantum computing poses an existential threat to classical public-key cryptographic systems, including RSA and Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC), through Shor's polynomial-time factorization algorithm. The Harvest Now, Decrypt Later (HNDL) attack paradigm further amplifies this threat by enabling adversaries to archive ciphertext today for future quantum-enabled decryption, rendering long-term data confidentiality immediately at risk. While the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) finalized post-quantum cryptographic standards ML-KEM (FIPS 203) and ML-DSA (FIPS 204) in August 2024, their practical integration into complete application-level communication systems remains a largely unaddressed research gap. This paper presents QuantumShield, a hybrid post-quantum secure peer-to-peer communication platform that integrates ML-KEM-768 for quantum-safe key encapsulation, ML-DSA-65 for authenticated digital signatures, and AES-256-GCM for high-throughput symmetric encryption. Our primary research contribution is a rigorous empirical analysis of PQC integration overhead in a real-world communication pipeline, quantifying latency, key size, and security trade-offs against classical RSA-2048 and ECC-256 baselines under controlled experimental conditions. Experimental evaluation across 1,000 iterations demonstrates that ML-KEM-768 encapsulation completes in 2.8 ± 0.2 ms compared to 4.1 ± 0.3 ms for ECDH key agreement — a 32% latency reduction while providing NIST Level 3 post-quantum security. The complete secure transfer pipeline processes 1 MB files in under 22 ms on commodity hardware. The system further provides interactive cryptographic visualization, adversary threat modeling, tamper detection simulation, and a hybrid migration framework demonstrating practical transition from classical to post-quantum infrastructure. QuantumShield establishes that quantum-safe communication is not merely theoretical but deployable today with negligible performance compromise.

title: Toward Quantum-Resilient PKI: A Systematic Literature Review of Post-Quantum Certificates Model
venue: Malaysian Journal of Science Health & Technology
abstract: The rise of quantum computing presents a critical threat to classical public-key cryptographic systems, necessitating a global shift toward post-quantum cryptography (PQC). While algorithmic standardisation has seen substantial progress since the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) initiated its call for PQC proposals in 2017, the integration of these algorithms into certificate-based infrastructures remains fragmented and underexplored. This gap creates uncertainty for secure communication, particularly in transitioning legacy systems into quantum-resilient environments. This systematic literature review (SLR) focuses on PQC certificate architectures studied between 2017 and 2025, encompassing the evolution of the field since NIST's formal standardisation efforts began. The review employs the PRISMA 2020 methodology to identify and analyse six distinct post-quantum certificate models: Pure PQC, Hybrid, Composite, Chameleon, Parallel, and Wrapped. Each model is evaluated across several criteria, including structure, backwards compatibility, tooling support, standardisation status, and production readiness, drawing evidence from scholarly publications, draft standards, and open-source implementations. Findings highlight the Hybrid certificate as the most viable short-term solution due to its high interoperability and maturity in deployment. Composite and Parallel architectures offer enhanced security assurances that are suitable for critical infrastructure, although they come with increased implementation complexity. Pure PQC certificates, while future-proof, are still limited to constrained or greenfield environments. Chameleon and Wrapped models are identified as emerging alternatives for blockchain and legacy scenarios, respectively, with limited but growing support. This review enlightens the design and deployment of quantum-safe public key infrastructures by outlining the trade-offs and maturity levels of each architecture. It also emphasises the need for continued development in standardisation and toolchain support to facilitate scalable and secure PQC adoption.

title: Quantum-Resistant Digital Certificates: A Hybrid PKI Framework Integrating PQC and QKD
venue: 2026 International Conference on Trends in Quantum Computing and Emerging Business Technologies (TQCEBT)
abstract: The advent of quantum computing offers the chance to increase the security of India's digital infrastructure, specifically the Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) under the Control of Certifying Authorities (CCA). For future-proofing digital certificates against quantum attacks, this paper proposes a hybrid PKI model that harmoniously merges Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) and Quantum Key Distribution (QKD). We investigate viable PQC algorithms, including lattice-based and hash-based cryptography, in combination with QKD for secured key exchange. Our solution is designed to provide adequate security without sacrificing backward compatibility with current systems. The hybrid PKI architecture outlined here is able to support integration of Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) and Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) to produce quantum-resistant digital certificates.

title: Dealing with the Post-Quantum Threat: Performance Considerations for Federal Public Key Infrastructure Systems
abstract: Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) continues to play a crucial role in securing government networks and providing cryptographic assurance of a person or device’s identity. Its strength depends on using a mathematically related public and private key, where the public key is intentionally shared, and the private key is controlled by an end entity to prove its identity. Quantum computers pose a risk to this paradigm, as they can perform mathematical operations much faster than classical computers. This could allow for quantum computers to derive an entity’s private key from their public key and perform operations while impersonating that entity. This report examines the role of PKI systems in the federal government of the United States (US), commonly used cryptographic algorithms throughout the US government, and how those algorithms could be made vulnerable to exploitation by the advancement of quantum computers. A comparison of the performance differences between Rivest-Shamir-Adleman (RSA), a cryptographic algorithm commonly utilized by Federal PKI systems, and the Post-Quantum Resistant (PQR) digital signature algorithm, CRYSTALS-Dilithium, is also provided. The report concludes with an analysis of the performance of PQR algorithms and considerations that federal agencies will need to make when implementing PKI systems that utilize PQR algorithms.

title: Hybridization of Post-Quantum Cryptography and Quantum Key Distribution: A Survey of Key Establishment Approaches
abstract: The emergence of quantum computing threatens classical cryptographic systems, motivating the development of cryptographic solutions based on Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) and Quantum Key Distribution (QKD). This paper surveys hybrid key-establishment techniques combining PQC and QKD, including XOR/concatenation, KEM combiners, split usage, and cascade approaches, and evaluates their applicability to protocols such as TLS and IPsec. It further compares positions of major standardization bodies (ANSSI, BSI, NCSC, NIST, ETSI) and identifies key challenges in standardization, performance, scalability, and complexity. While not a universal solution, hybridization remains relevant for high-assurance environments.

title: PQ-Derived Schnorr: Post-Quantum Hybrid Signature Scheme for Bitcoin-Compatible Networks
abstract: We present PQ-Derived Schnorr, a novel hybrid signature scheme that combines postquantum security with classical Bitcoin compatibility. Our approach leverages the CRYSTALS-Dilithium lattice-based signature scheme as the primary security foundation while maintaining full compatibility with existing Schnorr signature verification systems. The scheme implements a Dilithium First, Schnorr Derived philosophy, where the post-quantum component generates a challenge vector that serves as input to a classical Schnorr signature. This design ensures quantum resistance while preserving seamless integration with Bitcoin's Taproot and other Schnorr-based systems. While the total signature size is approximately 4.4 KB, the scheme is structurally optimized so that only a 64-byte Schnorr-compatible segment is required for verification on-chain in blockchain environments such as Bitcoin. Performance analysis shows signing times of 0.02-0.04 seconds, making it practical for real-world deployment. The scheme offers a modular path for post-quantum migration without requiring fundamental changes to existing Bitcoin infrastructure.

title: PQ-IDPS: Adversarially Robust Intrusion Detection for Post-Quantum Encrypted Traffic with Hybrid Classical-Quantum Machine Learning
abstract: The imminent deployment of post-quantum cryptography standards fundamentally transforms encrypted network traffic characteristics, rendering existing intrusion detection systems ineffective against traffic patterns generated by latticebased key encapsulation mechanisms and hash-based digital signatures. Although the National Institute of Standards and Technology finalized post-quantum cryptographic algorithms in August 2024, including ML-KEM based on CRYSTALS-Kyber and MLDSA based on CRYSTALS-Dilithium, contemporary intrusion detection approaches remain exclusively trained on classical TLS handshakes, creating critical security vulnerabilities during the cryptographic transition period. This paper introduces PQIDPS, a hybrid classical-quantum machine learning framework specifically designed for adversarially robust intrusion detection in post-quantum encrypted traffic environments. Our approach combines convolutional-LSTM architectures optimized for classical TLS with variational quantum classifiers that leverage quantum parallelism for post-quantum protocol analysis, unified through an adaptive ensemble mechanism that automatically detects protocol types and weights component contributions. To address the emerging threat of quantum-enhanced adversarial attacks, we develop a comprehensive defense framework incorporating Lipschitz-bounded network architectures, quantum noise injection during training, and randomized smoothing certification that provides provable robustness bounds against Grover-optimized perturbations. Through extensive evaluation on three novel datasets comprising CESNET-TLS-22 hybrid traffic, custom QUIC-PQC traces with pure Kyber key exchanges, and IoTPQC captures featuring Dilithium signatures, PQ-IDPS achieves 95.3% detection accuracy on hybrid classical-PQC traffic while maintaining certified robustness against quantum adversarial attacks bounded by O( √ N) Grover advantage. Our comprehensive ablation studies demonstrate that the quantum component contributes 7.8% accuracy improvement on pure post-quantum traffic compared to classical-only baselines, while hybrid ensemble fusion achieves 98.1% accuracy on protocol-mixed environments. The framework provides practical deployment guidelines for network operators transitioning to post-quantum cryptography, including traffic characterization tools, adversarial robustness benchmarks, and NIST migration recommendations. This work establishes the first comprehensive approach to adversarially robust intrusion detection for the post-quantum era, addressing both cryptographic modernization and quantum threat mitigation in a unified framework.

title: Hybrid Post-Quantum Cryptography and Quantum Key Distribution Co-Design for Quantum-Safe 6G, O-RAN, and IoT Infrastructure
venue: International Journal of Applied Smart Interdisciplinary Technologies
abstract: Cryptographically relevant quantum computers do not yet exist, but the transition away from classical public-key cryptography is already underway: adversaries can record encrypted traffic today and decrypt it once a sufficiently capable quantum computer becomes available, a threat known as harvest-now, decrypt-later. This paper examines the engineering case for combining post-quantum cryptography (PQC) with quantum key distribution (QKD) as a strategy for securing next-generation communication infrastructure, focusing on 6G core and radio-access networks, Open RAN (O-RAN), and constrained Internet of Things (IoT) deployments. Rather than treating the two mechanisms as symmetric, interchangeable layers, the paper examines what each one actually guarantees, surveys the empirical evidence available for deployment cost, and describes where national security authorities and standards bodies disagree on the value of QKD. The architecture is grounded in the finalized National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) PQC standards and its 2025 hybrid key-establishment guidance, drawing on empirical Open RAN latency and energy measurements published during 2025 and 2026, embedded-hardware benchmarks for constrained devices, and the small number of quantum key distribution deployments operating at metropolitan or national backbone scale today. The paper is explicit about which figures are measured results and which remain illustrative proposals, and it closes by naming the specific standardization and field-trial gaps that separate current practice from the architecture it describes. The purpose of the work is to give network architects and policymakers a single, evidence-graded reference for deciding where each mechanism belongs in a real deployment, rather than treating post-quantum and quantum-distributed keying as equivalent options.

title: Architecting Quantum-Resilient Blockchains: A Systems Framework for Post-Quantum Security, Governance, and Migration
abstract: Quantum computing poses a significant threat to blockchain systems that rely on elliptic curve cryptography and other classical security mechanisms. Algorithms such as Shor’s and Grover’s can weaken or completely break the cryptographic foundations of current blockchain networks, exposing them to risks including private key recovery, transaction forgery, consensus manipulation, and harvest-now-decrypt-later attacks. This paper presents a systems framework for designing quantum-resilient blockchains by integrating post-quantum cryptographic standards, threat modeling, architectural redesign, governance mechanisms, and migration planning. The study evaluates major post-quantum cryptographic primitives, assesses their suitability for blockchain environments, and proposes a layered architecture grounded in crypto-agility, defense-in-depth, and forward secrecy. A structured migration strategy is also introduced to support the transition of existing blockchain networks toward post-quantum security while maintaining operational continuity and stakeholder trust. The framework provides practical guidance for researchers, developers, and policymakers preparing blockchain ecosystems for the post-quantum era.

title: Performance and Security Analysis of Post-Quantum Signature Algorithms for Blockchain Systems
abstract: <i>The rise of large-scale quantum computing threatens the cryptographic foundations of blockchain networks. Current platforms depend on the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA), which Shor's algorithm can break in polynomial time. This paper presents a statistically rigorous performance and security comparison of three NIST-standardized postquantum signature schemes-Dilithium2 (ML-DSA, FIPS 204), Falcon-512 (FN-DSA), and SPHINCS+ (SLH-DSA, FIPS 205)benchmarked against ECDSA in a blockchain context. Using the liboqs C library (version 0.11.0), we executed 1 000 benchmark iterations per algorithm and measured key-generation, signing, and verification latency together with signature and public-key sizes, reporting 95 % bootstrap confidence intervals throughout. Dilithium2 achieves the fastest signing (0.093 ms) and verification (0.030 ms) of all evaluated schemes. Falcon-512 offers the most compact post-quantum signatures (655 bytes) with verification at 0.058 ms. SPHINCS+ provides the strongest cryptographic assurance, but its signing latency of 799.7 ms and 7 856-byte signatures carry a significant overhead. A blockchain simulation assuming 1 000 transactions per block shows that Dilithium2 and Falcon-512 reach estimated cryptographic throughputs of 33 445 and 17 271 transactions per second (TPS) respectively-well above ECDSA's 1 303 TPS-while SPHINCS+ falls to 695 TPS. Based on these findings we map each algorithm to concrete deployment scenarios and outline a hybrid migration strategy for the transition to a post-quantum blockchain ecosystem.</i>

title: Automated Post-Quantum Readiness Assessment for Internet-Facing TLS and PKI Infrastructure
abstract: Post-quantum migration is often framed as replacing a small set of public-key algorithms, yet operational infrastructures expose a broader systems problem: organizations must determine what cryptography they actually deploy, where it is used, how it relates to certificates and trust chains, what parts of the environment are exposed to harvest-now-decrypt-later (HNDL) threats, and which assets should be migrated first. This study develops a prototype assessment pipeline that converts externally observable TLS and certificate evidence into a structured cryptographic inventory, an explainable readiness score, and a migration-priority classification. The design is anchored in NIST's finalized FIPS 203-205 standards, NIST's cryptographic-agility and migration guidance, current U.S. inventory and migration requirements, and the 2026 IETF specifications for hybrid TLS 1.3 key establishment. Prior work by the author addresses HNDL mitigation and related migration considerations [22], while other related work addresses post-quantum PKI and certificate migration [23], digital signatures [24], hybrid TLS migration [25], and post-quantum TLS benchmarking [26]. Unlike a claim of universal quantum-readiness, the proposed score is explicitly a research model: substantive readiness dimensions are normalized to 0-100, while evidence confidence is reported separately to avoid conflating lack of observability with security. A controlled four-endpoint testbed was implemented with Python 3.13.5 and OpenSSL 3.5.5 and included TLS 1.3 with classical X25519, TLS 1.3 with ECDSA authentication, TLS 1.3 with X25519MLKEM768 hybrid key establishment, and TLS 1.2 with ECDHE-RSA. The prototype correctly identified the ground-truth TLS version, hybrid/non-hybrid status, and certificate key family for all four configurations. Mean local scan time was approximately 28.5 ms per endpoint over ten repetitions per configuration. These results demonstrate prototype feasibility, not enterprise-scale accuracy or performance. The main contribution is an auditable integration model linking inventory, evidence, risk dimensions, readiness, and migration actions; validation on larger, heterogeneous organizational environments remains necessary.

title: Post-Quantum Cryptographic Agility for Critical Internet Infrastructure: Architecture, Metrics, and Migration Strategies
abstract: Post-quantum migration is often described as an algorithm-replacement problem, but critical Internet infrastructure exposes a broader systems challenge: cryptographic dependencies span algorithms, keys, certificates, trust anchors, protocol stacks, libraries, hardware security modules, and legacy systems. This paper develops a proposed Post-Quantum Cryptographic Agility Framework (PQCAF) that treats those dependencies as one lifecycle-oriented control system. The framework integrates cryptographic asset discovery, dependency mapping, algorithm agility, key agility, certificate and PKI agility, protocol agility, legacy compatibility, migration governance, and continuous recovery capability. It introduces a measurable metric system built around Algorithm Replacement Time, Key Rotation Time, Certificate Replacement Time, PKI Coverage, Protocol Negotiation Success, Legacy Dependency Ratio, Inventory Coverage, Migration Automation Ratio, Recovery Time, and a proposed Cryptographic Agility Score (CAS). Rather than claiming an established universal score, the CAS is defined as a transparent research metric based on normalized dimensions and tested through sensitivity analysis. The paper also proposes a migration-priority model that jointly considers cryptographic exposure, data or authenticity lifetime, infrastructure criticality, Internet exposure, migration complexity, vendor dependency, and cost. Current NIST and IETF standards are used to anchor the technical architecture, including FIPS 203-205, current crypto-agility guidance, X.509 algorithm-identifier RFCs, and the August 2026 TLS 1.3 PQ/T hybrid standard. Evaluation uses clearly labeled illustrative scenarios rather than fabricated empirical results. The principal contribution is a unified measurement and decision framework intended to help organizations determine not only whether they have adopted post-quantum algorithms, but whether they can replace them again quickly and safely when requirements, algorithms, or threat conditions change.

title: Artificial Intelligence Powered and Blockchain Based Certificateless Authentication Internet of Vehicles
abstract: The Internet of Vehicles (IoV) is a key component of intelligent transport systems, supportingroad safety, traffic-congestion management, and self-driving vehicles. However, vehicular communication networks are open wireless environments vulnerable to impersonation, replay, man-in-the-middle, Sybil, and insider attacks. Existing authentication solutions based on certificateless cryptography, public-key infrastructure, or bilinear pairings suffer from high computation on on-board units (OBUs), depend upon certificate revocation, and provide no intelligent detection of behavioral network anomalies. Therefore, this article proposes an efficient, Artificial Intelligence (AI)-enabled, blockchain-driven certificateless authentication scheme for the IoV that combines three mutually reinforcing components: (i) an offline anomaly-detection subsystem based on Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI); (ii) a permissioned blockchain-based Hyperledger Fabric v2.5 that preserves the privacy and immutability of registration, authentication, and revocation logs; and (iii) a set of domain-separated hash function (SHA-256) combined with pseudorandom number generator (PRNG) aong with Exclusive-ORing (XOR) for the certificateless protocol design. Security analysis is accomplished via the Random Oracle Model (ROM), automated verification through ProVerif, and an informal analysis based on the Dolev-Yao (DY) adversary model guaranteeing session-key indistinguishability, mutual authentication, forward secrecy, vehicle anonymity, and pseudonym unlinkability. On a heterogeneous hardware testbed, the OBU completes authentication in 2.06 ms by consuming about 1.71 mJ of energy, which is 80% lower than the compared blockchain-based schemes. Hyperledger Fabric sustains a throughput of 1148 bits per second, and a linear complexity 𝑂(1) allows the system to scale up to 50,000 concurrently active vehicles without architectural changes.

title: Comment on “An advanced blockchain-based mutual authentication technique for the Internet of vehicles environment”: cryptanalysis and security vulnerabilities
abstract: Abstract  The Internet of Vehicles (IoV), in which vehicles exchange safety–critical information over open wireless channels, is characterized by large-scale, distributed operation, and stringent real-time constraints, requiring efficient and reliable communication mechanisms. Recently, Suyel et al. proposed a blockchain-based mutual authentication and key agreement protocol for IoV environments (The Journal of Supercomputing, 2025, https://doi.org/10.1007/s11227-025-07934-z ), claiming resistance against various attacks under the Dolev–Yao adversarial model. In this paper, we revisit the security of this protocol and demonstrate that its V2V authentication mechanism suffers from a fundamental design weakness. Specifically, the protocol verifies only the algebraic consistency of the received authentication tuple while accepting the verification key directly from the communication channel, without establishing a trustworthy binding between the claimed vehicle identity and the corresponding public key. As a consequence, an adversary can construct mathematically valid authentication messages using its own key pair while impersonating a legitimate vehicle. Based on this observation, we present several practical attacks, including vehicle impersonation, rogue public-key substitution, and message-substitution attacks. Furthermore, we show that the protocol relies on an auxiliary secure channel for final key confirmation, which contradicts the claimed Dolev–Yao threat model and weakens the overall security guarantees. To substantiate our findings, we provide a rigorous cryptanalytic evaluation combining algebraic validity analysis and BAN-logic reasoning. Our results reveal that the protocol fails to ensure reliable vehicle authentication and cannot securely attribute the established session key to the claimed peer identity. Consequently, the security claims of the target scheme do not hold under realistic adversarial conditions in IoV environments.

title: Certificateless Scheme Based NTRU Cryptosystem for Ad-Hoc UWB-IR Network
abstract: From the radar and military research world’s, the Ultra-WideBand Impulse Radio (UWB-IR) was adopted in the telecommunications world in the 1990’. Currently, the UWB-IR technology is an interesting candidate for close range Wireless Sensors Networks (WSNs). It is particularly attractive for industrial sensor networks due to its resilience to multipath interference, simple transceiver circuitry, accurate ranging ability, and low transmission power. In order to secure data and communications in the Ad-Hoc UWB-IR networks, UWB-IR requires suitable encryption protocols. In this paper, we review and summarize the IEEE 802.15.4 security sub-layer protocol of UWB-IR based Symmetric Key Cryptography scheme. Then, we highlight the different vulnerabilities and weaknesses present in this type of scheme. Finally, we prove, after a deep examination of multiple Public Key Cryptography (PKC) schemes, that the certificateless one is the most suitable for Ad-Hoc UWB-IR networks characterized by nodes mobility. Indeed, we have also evaluated and analyzed the different public key cryptosystems (PKCS) and concluded that NTRU is the most optimum public key cryptosystem to be used with the certificateless scheme in order to secure data and communications in Ad-Hoc UWB-IR Networks. This is due to the fact that it is the fastest PKCS to provide different security levels at a high speed with very constrained resources.

title: Certificate Verification in Dual Blockchain Model using Threshold Signature and Zero Knowledge Proofs
venue: 2025 IEEE 7th International Conference on Computing, Communication and Automation (ICCCA)
abstract: Certificate authentication in online systems is required to ensure integrity and authenticity and prevent forgery. Traditional blockchain-based approaches work with double-chain architecture without any privacy-preservation capability or pack whole certificates into a single chain and incur substantial storage overhead. In this study, we introduce a light-weight dual-blockchain architecture with an external verification and audit side-chain and an inner chain for offline storing certificates. Zero-Knowledge Succinct Non-Interactive Arguments of Knowledge (Zero Knowledge Proofs) are employed to sign hashes without revealing sensitive information, and threshold signatures are employed to sign certificates. Compared to the traditional single-chain and double-chain architecture, the proposed system realizes up to 30% lower latency and 25% higher throughput based on experimental results on 1,000–100,000 certificate dataset. These results indicate the efficiency, scalability, and privacy-preserving feature of the proposed solution, which can be applied to large-scale applications for certificate management.

title: DLSC: A double-layer blockchain consensus algorithm based on Schnorr threshold signatures for large-scale IoT systems
venue: Proceedings of the 2026 International Conference on Intelligent Internet of Things and Communication Technology
abstract: With the explosive growth of Internet of Things (IoT) devices, blockchain-based traceability systems are increasingly challenged by limited scalability, excessive communication overhead, and high computational burden in consensus procedures. To address these issues, this paper proposes a double-layer Schnorr threshold signature consensus algorithm, namely DLSC, for large-scale IoT environments. The proposed scheme adopts a hierarchical node architecture combined with a Schnorr threshold signature mechanism, where lower-layer nodes generate signature shares within each subgroup, while upper-layer nodes collaboratively complete global consensus. Compared with mainstream consensus protocols such as PBFT, DL-PBFT, HotStuff, and SBFT, DLSC maintains linear communication complexity of O(N) while significantly reducing the aggregation workload of leader nodes through hierarchical coordination. Theoretical analysis and simulation results demonstrate that DLSC achieves higher throughput, stronger fault tolerance, and lower resource consumption under large-scale IoT deployments. Therefore, it is well suited for resource-constrained blockchain traceability systems.

title: ROPSCON: Linear BFT From Schnorr Threshold Signatures
abstract: Existing linear Byzantine fault-tolerant (BFT) protocols heavily rely on Threshold Signatures (TS) to reduce communication complexity. The threshold signatures used and implemented in these BFT protocols should be non-interactive and all such schemes rely on heavy pairing operations. Threshold signatures using no pairings such as Schnorr TS are computationally more efficient but require multiple rounds of interaction and lack robustness. There has been a long-standing question on whether one could build more efficient BFT protocols from such pairing-free signatures. In this paper, we develop a novel approach that allows using threshold signatures like Schnorr TS in linear BFT protocols in an effective manner. In this approach, we can significantly reduce the interaction overhead caused by Schnorr TS while maintaining its computational efficiency. We instantiate a HotStuff-style BFT protocol called ROPSCON and show that ROPSCON achieves up to 2.2$\boldsymbol{\times}$× higher throughput compared to both HotStuff protocols using pairings as well as ones with directly aggregated signatures. The improvement is particularly evident in high-delay and low-bandwidth environments.

title: A Technical Review of FROST Threshold Signatures: Variants, Extensions, Security, and RFC9591
abstract: Threshold signature schemes enable a group of participants to collaboratively generate a signature if a subset of t out of n participants willingly participate in the signing process. Among recent developments, FROST (Flexible Round-Optimised Schnorr Threshold signatures) stands out for its efficiency, flexibility, and strong security guarantees in both theoretical and applied settings. This survey provides a comprehensive overview of FROST, starting from its cryptographic foundations in Schnorr signatures and the discrete logarithm problem to its formal security models and threat assumptions, including the unique robustness properties of FROST in the presence of malicious or aborting signers. We examine its two- round signing protocol, distributed key generation (DKG), and integration with secure multiparty computation frameworks. Furthermore, the survey categorises and analyses key extensions and adaptations of FROST, such as proactive and dynamic group configurations, post-quantum variants, compatibility with verifiable secret sharing, and deployments over alternative curves and signature primitives. We also evaluate practical implementations, standardisation efforts (e.g., by the IRTF CFRG), and real-world applications in blockchain and distributed systems. By mapping out current research and highlighting open challenges, this survey aims to guide future work in robust, scalable threshold signature protocols anchored in the FROST paradigm.

title: secp256k1-frost: Minimal-dependency RFC-9591 FROST threshold signing for secp256k1
abstract: Flexible Round-Optimized Schnorr Threshold Signatures (FROST), standardized in IETF RFC-9591, enable distributed generation of compact Schnorr signatures while preserving compatibility with existing secp256k1 verification workflows. This paper presents secp256k1-frost, a minimal-dependency implementation developed as an extension module for the secp256k1 library. The software explores how standardized threshold signing can be integrated into a production-grade elliptic-curve codebase by reusing audited primitives and maintaining portability through a C89 implementation. The project provides a practical platform for experimentation with standardized threshold cryptography in secp256k1-based systems. The implementation is open source and publicly available at https://github.com/bancaditalia/secp256k1-frost.

title: BMuSig2: Schnorr-Compatible Blind Multi-Signatures
venue: Proceedings of the ACM Asia Conference on Computer and Communications Security
abstract: Blind signatures and multi-signatures are well-known primitives, but blind multi-signatures (BMS), which combine both these primitives, were only recently formalized by Karantaidou et al. (CCS'24). A BMS scheme allows a user to obtain a compact signature on a common hidden message from a group of signers such that even if the signers collude, they cannot learn the message or link the final signature to any particular interaction. In this paper, we introduce BMuSig2, a 2-round concurrently secure blind multi-signature scheme whose signatures and verification match standard Schnorr signatures. This design enables systems using Schnorr signatures to adopt BMuSig2 as a drop-in replacement, requiring changes only to the issuance phase, while leaving verification unchanged. BMuSig2 builds on MuSig2 multi-signatures (CRYPTO'21) and integrates techniques from a recent blind signature scheme (CRYPTO'24) that leverages non-interactive zero-knowledge (NIZK) arguments and public-key encryption (PKE) to achieve concurrent security. We formally prove the security of BMuSig2 by relying on the unforgeability of MuSig2 and the security of the underlying NIZK and PKE components. We also provide a proof-of-concept implementation to demonstrate its practical efficiency.

title: A Robust and Efficient Threshold Signature Scheme Based on ECDSA
abstract: Threshold signatures serve as a cryptographic primitive fundamental to blockchain security and reliability. However, a significant limitation of existing ECDSA threshold signature protocols is their lack of robustness during the signing phase. Specifically, the presence of even a single malicious participant requires the termination of the protocol, thereby undermining the availability of the system. To address this critical issue, we present a novel robust threshold ECDSA signature scheme that guarantees uninterrupted operation even in the presence of adversarial participants. Our scheme consists of three distinct phases: distributed key generation, offline pre-signing and online signing. During the offline pre-signing phase, pre-signing shares are generated in advance to ensure fault-tolerant online signing. A key innovation of our approach is the offloading of computationally intensive operations to the offline phase, significantly optimizing the online signing efficiency. Security analysis demonstrates that our scheme achieves active security under the Strong RSA and Decisional Diffie-Hellman (DDH) assumptions. Compared to prior work, our solution not only ensures robustness but also reduces communication and computational overhead, making it particularly suitable for real-world blockchain deployments where both efficiency and fault tolerance are paramount.

title: Optimizing Threshold Secret Sharing with Hierarchical Access Structures in ECDSA
venue: 2024 IEEE International Conference on Internet of Things and Intelligence Systems (IoTaIS)
abstract: Secret sharing schemes divide sensitive information into multiple parts for secure distribution. The (t, n) threshold multi-secret sharing scheme based on Verifiable Secret Sharing (VSS) is a well-known method, but it typically uses a uniform access structure, which limits its application in organizations with hierarchical access needs. While hierarchical schemes often rely on a tree structure, this research explores a model where share values at each level directly relate to the secret.In this study, we employed three (t, n) threshold secret sharing schemes on the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA): one without a hierarchical access structure and two with hierarchical access structure. Performance analysis based on computation time and time complexity shows that hierarchical schemes outperform non-hierarchical one, as they reduce the polynomial degree into smaller hierarchical levels. Additionally, all three schemes were evaluated against the five core characteristics of digital signatures—authenticity, unforgeability, non-reusability, inalterability, and non-repudiation—and were found to satisfy these criteria.

title: Revolutionizing Security: A Dynamic Threshold Signature Scheme with Improved ECDSA
venue: 2024 7th International Seminar on Research of Information Technology and Intelligent Systems (ISRITI)
abstract: Blockchain technology enables secure, transparent, and decentralized systems, ideal for financial applications. However, its transparency can lead to vulnerabilities and privacy concerns. A dynamic threshold signature scheme offers a solution for asset monitoring within distributed systems. Bitcoin’s blockchain employs ECDSA, but its reliance on random k-values introduces weaknesses. To address this, we propose an improved ECDSA-based dynamic threshold signature scheme. We compare its performance and security against the original ECDSA-based scheme, finding minimal performance differences and a low probability of successful existential forgery attacks. This improved scheme offers a robust alternative for enhancing blockchain security.

title: DISTRIBUTED CERTIFICATE AUTHORITY IN CLUSTER-BASED MANET USING MULTI SECRET SHARING SCHEME
venue: Advances in Science and Technology Research Journal
abstract: Providing secure communications in mobile ad hoc networks (MANET) is an important and difficult problem, due to a lack of a key management infrastructure. The authentica tion is an important security service in (MANETs). To provide a node authentication service we use a fully distributed certificate authorities (FDCA) based on the threshold cryptography. In this paper we propose an efficient and verifiable multi secret sharing scheme in cluster-based MANET with a low computation system. Our scheme is based on the overdetermined linear system equation in Galois fields GF(2 r ). We have analyzed our scheme based on security and performance criteria, and compared with existing approaches. The efficiency of our proposed schemes was verified and evaluated by simula tion. Simulation results show that this approach is scalable.

title: Experimental Evaluation of Post-Quantum PKI Migration: Mixed Certificate Chains, Trust Anchors, and CA Strategies
abstract: Post-quantum migration of Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) is not equivalent to replacing a classical signature algorithm with a post-quantum alternative. Certificates, certification authorities (CAs), trust anchors, validation software, and relying-party trust stores form a dependency graph in which cryptographic changes propagate through multiple system layers. This paper extends a prior systematization of post-quantum PKI migration with a controlled experimental study of X.509 certificate chains. Using OpenSSL 3.5.5 on a Debian amd64 environment, the experiment constructs classical RSA-2048 and ECDSA P-256 chains, pure ML-DSA-44/65/87 and SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s/128f chains, and two mixed-algorithm transitional chains. Certificate sizes are measured from DER encodings, and certification-path validation is benchmarked with repeated OpenSSL verification runs. The measured results show substantial certificate-chain expansion for standardized post-quantum signatures relative to the ECDSA baseline: the transmitted two-certificate chain grows from 1,090 bytes for ECDSA P-256 to 8,314 bytes for ML-DSA-44, 11,373 bytes for ML-DSA-65, 15,288 bytes for ML-DSA-87, 16,685 bytes for SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s, and 35,150 bytes for SLH-DSA-SHA2-128f. Validation latency increases more moderately in the tested process-level benchmark, with median times from 3.64 ms for ML-DSA-44 to 5.02 ms for SLH-DSA-SHA2-128f, compared with 3.57 ms for ECDSA. Mixed chains validate successfully in the tested implementation, but require multiple cryptographic families and therefore retain migration dependencies that a size-only metric cannot capture. The results indicate that certificate-chain expansion and trust-anchor storage growth are more pronounced engineering effects than path-validation latency in this controlled environment. The paper concludes with evidence-based migration recommendations, a controlled configuration framework, and explicit limitations concerning implementation scope, hardware, interoperability, and production-scale deployment.

title: An Integrated Group Signature and Chameleon Hash Framework for Effective, Secure, and Private VANET Communication
abstract: Abstract VANET (Vehicular Ad hoc Networks) enable on-road wireless communication using vehicular and road-based electronic infrastructure. The services provided include routine traffic information dissemination aimed at ensuring safe driving while offering payment systems, and entertainment services are also part of VANET services. Ensuring secure, cost-effective VANET communication is a key research focus. A mechanism for unidentified message transmission, reciprocal vehicular and road base verification, as well as highly secure authentication by a trusted party, preservation of confidentiality of messages, recovery of the identity of vehicle by a trusted authority in unfortunate events, and low set up cost, is the prerequisite for trusted vehicular communication in VANET. The technique of Chameleon hashing signature provides message security with frequent changing of keys. The validation of vehicular identity in group-based communication is centralized using group signature and time stamping. This study proposes a framework combining chameleon hash signatures with group signatures to enhance VANET communication privacy, security, and cost-effectiveness.

title: CTR-M: A Certificate-Trust-Reliability Messaging Framework with Timed Operational Semantics for Secure Autonomous V2X Communication
venue: 2026 International Conference on Artificial Intelligence, Computer, Data Sciences and Applications (ACDSA)
abstract: Vehicular communication networks must ensure that the messages exchanged between vehicles need to be authentic, timely, and reliable. The existing V2X security schemes emphasize cryptographic validation but they rarely focus on how delay, behavioral trust, and wireless conditions collectively influence reliability. To address these limitations, we propose the Certificate-Trust-Reliability Messaging (CTR-M) framework, where interactions between vehicles are modelled as a time behavior - driven dependent communication process. The framework combines certificate verification, adaptive trust estimation, and delay-based filtering to safeguard secure and dependable message flow. Formal verification using UPPAAL shows that CTR-M shows stable trust behavior and timely message delivery even in the presence of DoS and MiM attacks.

title: A HYBRID IDENTITY AUTHENTICATION SYSTEM COMBINING PHYSICAL LAYER RECOGNITION AND CERTIFICATES FOR C-V2X IN HIGHWAY ENVIRONMENTS
abstract: With the rapid development of Cellular Vehicle-to-Everything (C-V2X) communication systems, ensuring the security and integrity of data exchanged between vehicles and infrastructure has become a significant challenge. Identity authentication plays a crucial role in safeguarding these communications against threats such as identity spoofing and data tampering. Traditional certificate-based authentication methods, while effective, often suffer from performance issues, especially in high-speed, dynamic environments such as highways. In this paper, we propose a hybrid identity authentication system that combines physical layer recognition with certificate-based methods to enhance security and improve real-time performance in C-V2X systems operating in highway environments. The physical layer authentication leverages channel state information (CSI), signal fingerprints, and other radio-frequency characteristics to authenticate vehicles, providing an additional layer of security. This is combined with certificate-based public key infrastructure (PKI) to offer a comprehensive and robust identity verification process. The hybrid approach addresses the shortcomings of traditional methods by enhancing security while minimizing computational overhead and ensuring low-latency authentication. We discuss the challenges and opportunities in integrating these two authentication methods and highlight the potential impact of emerging technologies, such as 5G and machine learning, in optimizing the hybrid authentication process for C-V2X systems. Finally, we propose future research directions to further improve the efficiency, scalability, and robustness of hybrid authentication schemes in vehicular networks.

title: Performance and Scalability of Hybrid Post-Quantum TLS 1.3 on Edge IoT Platforms under Concurrent-Client Load
abstract: As Transport Layer Security (TLS) 1.3 migrates to quantum-resistant hybrid post-quantum cryptography (PQC), a growing population of edge Internet of Things (IoT) devices must terminate these heavier handshakes on their own. Yet how hybrid PQC-TLS performs and scales on this intermediate, Linux-class tier of hardware, between the constrained microcontrollers and the capable cloud serversthat the literature has already measured, has been left largely uncharacterized. We close that gap with a controlled performance and scalability study of hybrid PQC-TLS 1.3 on two representative edge platforms, the NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano and the Raspberry Pi 4B, sweeping NIST security categories L1/L2 through L5 and concurrent-client loads from 5 to 50, with per-stage instrumentation that separates cryptographic computation from protocol-stack and request-handling overhead. Three results stand out. First, the cryptography is not the bottleneck: lattice operations account for only 2–5% of handshake latency, while the protocol-stack and request-handling cost of moving the enlargedhybrid certificate, key share, and signature payloads dominates. Second, latency scales super-linearly beyond roughly 20 concurrent clients, by 7.5–10.8×, with the 95th-percentile-to-mean ratio widening from 1.4–1.7 to 2.0–2.2, even though neither endpoint approaches CPU or memory saturation, which pins the limit on request-handling contention rather than resource exhaustion. Third, hardware capability does not map cleanly to performance: a faster per-core clock makes the nominally weaker Raspberry Pi 4B 5–25% quicker than the accelerator-equipped Jetson Orin Nano at L1, an advantage that vanishes by L5. With mean handshake durations below one second in every configuration tested, hybrid PQC-TLS 1.3 is already practical at the edge; the real target for scalable deployment is the request-handling architecture, not the cryptographic primitives.

title: Assessing and Managing Post-Quantum Migration Readiness Across TLS and PKI Infrastructure
abstract: Post-quantum migration is an infrastructure transition rather than a simple substitution of cryptographic algorithms. Public-key mechanisms used in TLS, certificates, certificate authorities, digital signatures, key-management systems, and trust stores create dependencies that can make migration difficult to sequence and validate. This paper develops a literature-based readiness and migration framework that connects cryptographic discovery, dependency mapping, Harvest Now, Decrypt Later (HNDL) exposure, TLS and PKI assessment, migration prioritization, interoperability validation, and cryptographic agility. The analysis uses current NIST standards and migration material, NIST's 2026 crypto-agility guidance, IETF specifications, and a set of peer-reviewed studies on post-quantum TLS, PKI migration, HNDL risk, and migration frameworks. It also incorporates recent infrastructure-oriented work by Hridoy Roy where accessible full text or verified bibliographic records establish direct relevance to the cited claim. The contribution is a conceptual framework, not a new benchmark or production measurement study. The paper therefore distinguishes established standards and guidance from research claims and from the framework proposed here. The resulting model treats readiness as a lifecycle capability: organizations must be able to discover cryptography, understand dependencies, prioritize long-lived and high-value assets, test transition mechanisms, deploy replacements, retire vulnerable mechanisms, and retain the ability to change algorithms again.

title: Beyond the Handshake: PSKs, Session Resumption, and KeyUpdate in Post-Quantum TLS Migration
abstract: Post-quantum migration of Transport Layer Security (TLS) is frequently framed as the replacement of classical key-exchange mechanisms with post-quantum alternatives. That framing is incomplete because TLS 1.3 derives security through a sequence of secrets and lifecycle mechanisms that extend beyond the initial handshake. In particular, pre-shared keys (PSKs), session resumption, 0-RTT operation, and the KeyUpdate mechanism can alter the security properties obtained from an initial post-quantum or hybrid exchange. This paper examines how these mechanisms should be interpreted and managed during post-quantum TLS migration. A structured literature and standards analysis is conducted using TLS 1.3 specifications, recent IETF work on hybrid key exchange and ML-KEM, NIST post-quantum standards, security guidance, and recent post-quantum TLS research, including Roy's systematization of TLS migration. The analysis distinguishes the provenance of keying material, the presence or absence of fresh asymmetric key establishment, forward-secrecy properties, post-compromise implications, and the relationship between trafficsecret evolution and independent post-quantum key establishment. The resulting framework shows that "post-quantum TLS" cannot be treated as a binary property of a connection. A deployment may use a post-quantum or hybrid initial handshake while retaining resumption paths, PSK-only modes, or traffic-secret updates whose security properties differ materially from those of a fresh hybrid handshake. The paper proposes a lifecycle-oriented classification and migration decision framework that treats fresh hybrid key establishment, PSK resumption, 0-RTT, and KeyUpdate as separate security controls. The contribution is conceptual and evidence-based; it does not claim new experimental measurements.

title: A Readiness and Maturity Framework for Post-Quantum TLS Adoption
abstract: Transport Layer Security (TLS) protects most Internet traffic, yet migration to post-quantum TLS (PQ-TLS) depends on more than publishing a new algorithm standard. Despite rapid standardization of the Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism (ML-KEM) and hybrid TLS groups, practitioners lack a structured way to assess whether deployment ecosystems are ready to adopt PQ-TLS. This letter proposes a six-dimensional readiness and adoption framework and a reproducible maturity rubric (levels 0--4). A case study of Windows, Linux, macOS, and Android applies the rubric to cited vendor documentation. The main finding is that cryptographic and protocol readiness are uniformly high across the case study, while platform and application readiness show the widest gap and act as the primary adoption bottlenecks for software that inherits OS TLS APIs. The study reports documented transition signals, not live PQ-TLS negotiation rates.

title: Who Gets Post-Quantum TLS? Measuring Thai Personal-Data and Popular Hosts
abstract: Personal data that must stay confidential for decades, such as tax, health and identity records, is exposed to ”harvest now, decrypt later”: traffic recorded today could be decrypted once quantum computers mature. Hybrid post-quantum key exchange for TLS is enabled by default in major browsers, content delivery networks (CDNs) and OpenSSL, but existing measurements count domains or homepages rather than the hosts that carry personal data. We measured 288 Thai banks, insurers, hospitals, government agencies and regulators from two networks, including web endpoints coded as handling personal data and service hosts referenced by 20 banking and government apps, and 1,040 popular .th hosts drawn from the Chrome UX Report. Post-quantum key exchange followed the TLS terminator: 97.4% of organisational web hosts behind a CDN negotiated it, against 3.6% of other hosts, and 98.1% against 7.5% among popular hosts. Only about 40% of popular hosts carrying personal data were protected, and hosts classified as institutional channels, such as hospital claims systems, appeared least protected (7–17%), though concentrated in a few organisations. Service hosts referenced in apps were protected far less often than the same apps&apos; content hosts (30.9% against 66.1%), while web data endpoints usually matched their organisation&apos;s homepage. Protection also differed by CDN product, and most classical hosts outside a CDN already used TLS 1.3. For regulators and auditors, the findings imply testing data-bearing hosts rather than homepages and documenting reliance on supplier defaults.

title: PQC-OAV: A Unified Evidential Assurance Framework for Post-Quantum Transport (TLS, SSH, QUIC)
abstract: The transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography introduces critical observability challenges. Large hybrid keys and encapsulated ciphertexts systematically disrupt traditional network monitoring tools. Existing solutions rely on fragmented, protocol-specific parsers that fail to provide a cohesive view of cryptographic compliance across the diverse landscape of modern secure transport. This paper generalizes the PQC-OAV architecture to establish a strictly protocol-agnostic, passive assurance framework. We define a formal Unified Tuple (Ts), a normalized feature vector that maps disparate protocol identifiers into a canonical format. This includes the TLS key_share extension, the SSH KEXINIT message, and QUIC Initial and handshake negotiation artifacts carrying the inner TLS handshake. We validate this methodology by implementing a Hybrid Architecture that converges traffic generation from production-grade OpenSSL v3.5.0, OQS-OpenSSH v9.8, and quic-go v0.59.0 engines with a unified passive normalization engine. Our analysis executed an exhaustive combinatorial matrix of 12,600 test conditions, yielding a finalized dataset of 12,300 viable transport sessions. Under adverse network conditions (incorporating up to 20 percent packet loss, bivariate datagram reordering, and restrictive MTU constraints), we identify precise protocol survivability boundaries. We demonstrate that while TCP stacks suffer severe latency compounding under post-quantum loads, UDP multiplexing maintains robust resilience on standard links but undergoes complete structural collapse under constrained MTUs, accounting for 300 socket-layer rejections. We confirm that PQC-OAV achieves deterministic session-level normalization fidelity and rule consistency within these tested parameters. This result establishes that the framework successfully restores unified observability to the post-quantum network stack and identifies predictable structural invariants that enable the passive classification of hybrid implementation strategies.

title: Evaluating Post-Quantum TLS Performance for the Internet of Things Using Raspberry Pi Devices
venue: 2026 IEEE International Workshop on Metrology for Industry 4.0 & IoT (MetroInd4.0 & IoT)
abstract: Post-Quantum Cryptography is approaching deployment in TLS, raising important questions for the IoT, where large numbers of long-lived and resource-constrained edge devices must remain secure over decades. Many IoT systems rely on low-cost, Linux-capable edge nodes with limited compute, memory, and power resources, making post-quantum TLS a systems-level concern rather than a purely cryptographic one. This paper benchmarks representative classical and post-quantum TLS primitives on Raspberry Pi 1, 3, 4, used as proxies for constrained IoT edge devices bridging microcontrollers and cloud infrastructure. Performance is evaluated in terms of latency, hardware counters, cache behaviour, and peak resident memory across relevant message sizes. Results show that lightweight symmetric primitives such as Ascon-128 consistently outperform traditional TLS AEADs, while ML-KEM-512 and hybrid signature configurations provide the most balanced trade-offs among post-quantum public-key schemes. A PQC-enabled TLS-like handshake introduces modest overhead on modern IoT-class hardware but significantly higher cost on older platforms, highlighting the impact of device heterogeneity in deployed IoT fleets. Overall, the results demonstrate that post-quantum TLS is feasible on contemporary IoT edge hardware when algorithms are carefully selected, providing practical guidance for quantum-safe IoT deployments.

title: When Hybrid TLS Is Not Enough: Parser Robustness, API Exposure, and Policy Drift in Post-Quantum TLS 1.3
venue: 2026 IEEE Conference on Communications and Network Security (CNS)
abstract: Hybrid post-quantum (PQ) key exchange is deployed at scale in TLS 1.3, typically combining X25519 with ML-KEM-768 in a single key_share. TLS 1.3’s transcript authentication forecloses ordinary on-path negotiation tampering, and prior work has measured the performance cost of PQ cryptography. We argue that hybrid PQ TLS may still be insufficient in practice, not for cryptographic reasons but at the deployment envelope: parser edge cases for hybrid key_share payloads, draft-era identifier coexistence, opaque APIs that prevent applications from enforcing “hybrid or fail,” permissive defaults, and TLS-terminating middleboxes that legitimately negotiate classical traffic in front of PQ-capable backends. We make four contributions: (i) a threat-model-aware taxonomy that separates external-MITM attacks (cryptographically infeasible against TLS 1.3) from malicious-endpoint parser abuse, legitimate-terminator policy fallback, and configuration drift; (ii) a differential conformance harness that measures malformed hybrid key_share handling across four PQ-capable TLS stacks (OpenSSL+oqs-provider, Rustls, AWS-LC, wolfSSL); (iii) an API-exposure audit on the same four stacks; (iv) Negoguard, a prototype evidence-aware policy verifier illustrated on a synthetic decision-boundary corpus and on captured network traffic from a hybrid baseline and a split-termination fallback. Our central empirical finding is that hybrid parser robustness across the tested stacks is better than feared: all four stacks rejected every malformed or degenerate hybrid input we tested. The remaining deployment risk is not silent parser acceptance but the inability of applications and operators to uniformly observe and enforce the negotiated PQ state across stacks and split-termination boundaries.

title: Performance Evaluation of Post-Quantum Cryptography in IoT: A Case Study on MQTT Over TLS Under Network Constraints
venue: 2026 14th International Symposium on Digital Forensics and Security (ISDFS)
abstract: The imminent advent of quantum computing poses a significant threat to current asymmetric cryptographic standards, such as RSA and Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC), widely used in Internet of Things (IoT) protocols. This paper evaluates the performance impact of migrating to Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) in an MQTT (Message Queuing Telemetry Transport) environment secured by TLS. We propose a reproducible benchmark framework based on containerization (Docker) and hardware emulation (QEMU/ARM64) to simulate resource-constrained IoT devices. We compared the handshake latency of standard TLS against a hybrid implementation utilizing NIST-standardized PQC algorithms: ML-KEM-768 (Key Encapsulation) and ML-DSA-65 (Digital Signature). Experiments conducted under controlled network impairments (latency, jitter, and packet loss) revealed that PQC introduces an approximate 4.7x increase in connection establishment time compared to classical TLS, primarily due to computational overhead on the ARM64 architecture. However, message publication latency posthandshake remains negligible. These findings suggest that while PQC is viable for IoT, it necessitates architectural shifts towards persistent sessions to mitigate initial handshake costs.

title: A Quantum-Agile Framework for Secure 5G Core Communication Using Post-Quantum TLS
venue: ICC 2026 - IEEE International Conference on Communications
abstract: The rise of quantum computing poses a critical threat to current cryptographic protocols, particularly RSA and Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC), which are vulnerable to attacks such as Shor’s algorithm. As 5G networks rely heavily on public key infrastructure, the risk of compromise in the quantum era is significant. Transitioning to post-quantum cryptographic (PQC) primitives is therefore an urgent priority. This paper presents a practical framework for integrating PQC into 5G control plane communication, specifically over Service-Based Interfaces (SBIs). Using the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) finalist algorithm Dilithium3, we implement PQC-enabled Transport Layer Security (TLS) handshakes via a modular proxy built in Python. The proxy intercepts inter-service traffic and offloads cryptographic operations to a containerized environment using liboqs. Importantly, this integration does not require altering existing 5G functions. System-level metrics, including CPU (Central Processing Unit) usage, memory, latency, and jitter, were benchmarked before and after PQC integration. Results show performance overhead remains within acceptable bounds, confirming deployment viability. This work proposes a hybrid migration strategy that enables backward compatibility and cryptographic agility. It provides a scalable and testable foundation for securing 5G networks in the quantum era while aligning with emerging European Telecommunications Standards Institute (ETSI) and NIST guidelines for post-quantum transition.

title: Beyond Random-Split Accuracy: Duplicate-Safe and Crypto-Agile Evaluation of Anomaly Detection for Post-Quantum TLS
abstract: Post-quantum cryptography changes the size, timing, and algorithmic context of Transport Layer Security (TLS) handshakes, creating a dynamic normal class for anomaly detectors. This study evaluates an assurance framework, rather than proposing a new classifier, on CIC-PQC_OAV v1: 40,010 sessions represented by 32 encrypted-metadata features. An audit finds 185 exact fingerprints shared across the supplied partitions, affecting 1594 sessions, plus one exact conflicting-label group. We compare the fixed split with five-seed, size-matched sample-stratified, exact-disjoint, raw round-3-disjoint, and IQR-normalized round-3-disjoint protocols, each separating fitting, probability calibration, threshold selection, conformal calibration, and testing. The fixed-split LightGBM F1 is 0.9013; controlled five-seed means cluster at 0.8872–0.8898, showing that its gap is not attributable solely to duplicate control. Condition-disjoint tests reveal heterogeneous anomaly transfer and false-positive rates of 0.9998, 0.9897, and 0.6107 for three unseen valid families. Isotonic calibration yields a Brier score of 0.0221±0.0013, while five-seed perturbations confirm sensitivity to timing masking and byte scaling. The results support layered, dataset-bounded evaluation combining fingerprint independence, condition holdouts, calibration, selective review, robustness, and explanation.

title: Crypto-Agile migration to Hybrid Post-Quantum Cryptography in Enterprise TLS PKI VPN and Cloud-Native Systems and services
abstract: The transition to post-quantum cryptography presents enterprises with a complex systems-engineering challenge extending beyond algorithm replacement. Transport Layer Security, public key infrastructure, virtual private networks, cloud-native platforms, identity services, and machine-to-machine communications depend on interconnected cryptographic libraries, certificates, protocols, hardware modules, policies, and vendor products. This review examines crypto-agile migration to hybrid post-quantum cryptography, where classical and quantum-resistant mechanisms are combined to preserve established assurance while emerging algorithms and implementations mature. It develops a migration-oriented taxonomy covering cryptographic discovery, dependency mapping, hybrid key establishment, composite authentication, certificate lifecycle management, protocol negotiation, performance optimization, interoperability testing, and operational governance. Particular attention is given to larger keys, ciphertexts, and signatures; handshake fragmentation; certificate-chain expansion; hardware acceleration; legacy compatibility; downgrade resistance; and observability across distributed environments. The review compares migration requirements in enterprise TLS, PKI, remote-access and site-to-site VPNs, service meshes, API gateways, container platforms, serverless services, secrets systems, and multicloud infrastructures. It also analyzes staged deployment patterns, including inventory-first modernization, proxy-based termination, dual certificates, hybrid tunnels, algorithm-policy abstraction, and controlled fallback. Evaluation criteria integrate security, interoperability, latency, throughput, bandwidth, memory, certificate issuance, operational resilience, and rollback readiness. The findings indicate that successful migration depends on treating cryptography as a continuously governed enterprise capability rather than a fixed protocol configuration. The paper concludes by identifying gaps in standardization, automated discovery, cross-vendor testing, cryptographic telemetry, constrained-device support, and lifecycle evidence, providing organizations with a structured foundation for prioritized, reversible, and verifiable post-quantum transformation across heterogeneous digital services. Keywords: Crypto-Agility, Hybrid Cryptography, Post-Quantum Cryptography, Public Key Infrastructure, Quantum-Safe Migration, Transport Layer Security.

title: HCASS: Hybrid Certificateless Aggregate Signcryption Scheme for Post-Quantum Migration of ICS
abstract: As the backbone of critical national infrastructure, Industrial Control Systems (ICS) operate with decades-long lifecycles. Coupled with the integration of the Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT), this makes their immediate migration to post-quantum cryptography essential to counter the fundamental threat posed by the rapid advancement of quantum computing. However, lattice-based primitives often present challenges in meeting the sub-millisecond latency requirements of deterministic control loops. We propose HCASS, a Hybrid Certificateless Aggregate Signcryption Scheme for the post-quantum migration of ICS devices. During the key generation phase, we design a diagonal trapdoor structure that reduces the complexity of preimage sampling from O(k^2) to O(k), where k is the gadget dimension parameter determined by the modulus q. To ensure real-time responsiveness, HCASS utilizes an offline/online decomposition strategy, shifting 90.9% of the computation to a precomputation stage and achieving an online signcryption latency of 0.855 ms. Furthermore, we implement an edge-assisted aggregation mechanism to compress signature-related communication from O(N) to O(1), where N denotes the number of participating devices. Evaluation shows that HCASS reduces the normalized receiver-side verification cost by 92.6% compared to independent signcryption while maintaining IND-CCA2 and EUF-CMA security. This construction provides a practical approach for securing data transmission in resource-constrained industrial infrastructures.

title: Integrating Post-Quantum Cryptography Into a CDN-Style PKI: Design, Trade-Offs, and an Experimental Baseline
abstract: Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) adds larger certificates and extra workload to the Transport Layer Security (TLS) handshake. In order to analyze the effect of that change on content delivery, a controlled testbed with conditions replicating a Content Delivery Network (CDN) is used. The system uses a standard X. 509 certificate chain over TLS 1.3. It compares RSA with legacy key exchange, RSA with hybrid key encapsulation mechanism (KEM), and Module Lattice-based Digital Signature Algorithm (ML-DSA) with hybrid KEM. The test harness generates and provides certificates and establishes TLS parameters. The test harness also supports mixed web workloads and records key metrics, including handshake time, page and object latency, throughput, and server CPU utilization. Experiments consist of hot and cold cache scenarios as well as new and keep-alive connections. Across the matrix, the session establishment cost increases under hybrid and PQC suites, while steady-state delivery is dominated by caching and connection reuse. CPU load is concentrated at the edge, and certificate chains remain within routine CDN limits.

title: Designing a Quantum-Resistant Hierarchical Hybrid Authentication and Dynamic Fallback Mechanism for Enterprise PKI
venue: 2025 5th International Conference on Computer Science and Blockchain (CCSB)
abstract: To address the threat posed by quantum algorithms to traditional public-key cryptography and manage the coexistence of classical and post-quantum cryptographic (PQC) algorithms during the PKI post-quantum migration transition period, this paper proposes a scalable hierarchical hybrid authentication scheme. By extending and enhancing traditional certificates using multiple signature algorithms, the scheme improves performance while ensuring security. The scheme was experimentally validated based on a four-l PKI certificate chain model. To improve compatibility with multiple algorithms coexisting during the transition to post-quantum cryptography, this paper designs a dynamic fallback mechanism and proposes optimization schemes based on experimental results. Comprehensive performance testing was conducted under the TLS 1.3 protocol. The results demonstrate that: (a)The hierarchical hybrid authentication scheme achieves significantly improved handshake performance compared to a pure PQC solution; (b) The dynamic fallback mechanism has a 100 per cent successful connection rate and has good feasibility.
